content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'virgin' functions symbolically as an image of purity and undivided covenant faithfulness to God. Corporately, God's people (Israel as 'virgin daughter Zion' in the Old Testament; the Church in the New Testament) are pictured as a virgin betrothed to God/Christ, with virginity signifying freedom from spiritual adultery (idolatry, apostasy) and readiness for union with the divine Bridegroom. The term is thus read primarily as a marital-covenant metaphor: the pure, faithful bride awaiting her husband.", "primary_basis": ["2 Corinthians 11:2 (Paul presents the church 'as a pure virgin to Christ')", "Revelation 14:4 (the 144,000 'are virgins,' widely read as undefiled faithfulness rather than literal celibacy)", "Matthew 25:1-13 (parable of the ten virgins awaiting the bridegroom)", "Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:22-23 and Luke 1:26-35 (the virgin who conceives, applied to Mary)", "2 Kings 19:21; Isaiah 37:22 ('virgin daughter of Zion')", "Jeremiah 18:13; 31:4, 21 ('virgin Israel')", "Amos 5:2; Lamentations 1:15; 2:13 (virgin Israel/Zion in lament)", "Revelation 19:7-8; 21:2, 9 (the bride of the Lamb, pure and prepared)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Christological/Mariological reading: the virgin of Isaiah 7:14 as a literal prophetic sign fulfilled in the virginal conception of Jesus by Mary, signifying the divine origin and sinlessness of Christ; in Catholic and Orthodox tradition Mary's perpetual virginity further symbolizes her total consecration and figures the Church.", "basis": ["Isaiah 7:14", "Matthew 1:18-25", "Luke 1:26-38"], "prominence": "dominant"}, {"meaning": "Critical-scholarly and Jewish reading: the Hebrew 'almah' in Isaiah 7:14 means 'young woman' rather than technical 'virgin,' with the sign originally referring to a child born in Isaiah's own time (e.g., Hezekiah or Isaiah's son); the virgin-birth reading arises from the Septuagint's 'parthenos.'", "basis": ["Isaiah 7:14-16 in historical context", "Isaiah 8:3-4", "Septuagint rendering of Isaiah 7:14"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Ascetic/vocational reading: virginity as a consecrated state of life superior to or alongside marriage, symbolizing total devotion to God and anticipation of the resurrection life; foundational for consecrated virgins, monasticism, and clerical celibacy in Catholic and Orthodox traditions.", "basis": ["1 Corinthians 7:25-38", "Matthew 19:10-12", "Revelation 14:4 read literally by some Fathers"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Eschatological readiness reading: the virgins of Matthew 25 symbolize professing believers whose preparedness (oil/lamps) determines entry to the wedding feast; emphasis falls on watchfulness rather than purity per se.", "basis": ["Matthew 25:1-13"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Literal celibacy reading of Revelation 14:4: the 144,000 are actual unmarried celibates, taken by some patristic writers and some sectarian groups (e.g., certain Adventist or restorationist readings) rather than a metaphor for spiritual fidelity.", "basis": ["Revelation 14:1-5"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Mary as type or icon of the Church: the Virgin Mother prefigures the Church, which is both virgin (pure in faith) and mother (bearing children through baptism), a patristic theme (e.g., Ambrose, Augustine) formalized in Catholic ecclesiology.", "basis": ["Luke 1:26-38", "John 19:26-27", "Revelation 12:1-6 as read Mariologically/ecclesiologically"], "prominence": "common"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "The term operates on two well-established registers that interpreters generally treat as complementary rather than competing: (1) the literal-prophetic virginity of Mary (Isaiah 7:14/Matthew 1) and (2) the symbolic virgin-bride motif for God's people (2 Corinthians 11:2; Revelation 14; the OT 'virgin Israel/Zion' texts). The corporate purity/faithfulness meaning is the standard answer when 'virgin' is treated as a symbol, since the Marian usage is normally treated as historical fact and prophetic sign rather than symbol. The main genuine dispute in scholarship concerns the translation of 'almah' in Isaiah 7:14, and in Revelation 14:4 whether 'virgins' is literal or figurative; neither dispute unsettles the broad consensus that virginity in Scripture connotes purity and exclusive fidelity to God."}
